title: Picot
subtitle: A tiny chain loop that trims an edge with little bumps
excerpt: A picot is a small loop of chains closed back on itself, making a neat bump along an edge. It is the classic crochet trim: a row of picots turns a plain border into a scalloped, decorative one without much extra work.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passages on picots used to ornament crochet edges. Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The picot carries the same name in UK and US terminology.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small decorative loop made by working a few chains and then closing them back into the base of the first chain, leaving a little bump that trims an edge.
The simplest crochet stitch, made by drawing the yarn through the loop on the hook. A picot is built from a short run of chains.
The shortest crochet stitch, drawn straight through both the work and the loop on the hook. It is one of the ways to close a picot loop back on itself.

content.text: stitches closed back on itself, sitting up off the edge as a small bump. Worked in a row, picots turn a plain border into a softly scalloped one. They are the most common crochet trim, the finishing touch on edgings, collars, and the points of lace.
Work along an edge until you reach the point where the picot should sit. This is the common three-chain picot.
Insert the hook back into the base of those chains, into the front loop and the side strand of the stitch you started from.
. A small firm bump pops up off the edge.
Continue along the edge to the next picot point and repeat.
Space the picots evenly, usually two or three stitches apart, so the scallops sit regular along the border.

Picots finish the free edge of edgings, the necklines and cuffs of garments, the points of doilies, and the joins between lace motifs. A single round of picots is often all it takes to lift a plain piece into something that looks finished. They also work as small joining loops, where the picot of one motif links to the picot of the next as you go.

A picot can be two, three, four, or five chains depending on how large a bump you want. Closing it with a double crochet instead of a slip stitch gives a firmer, more upright picot. A picot worked into the middle of a chain loop makes the decorative tips of a lace edging. The picot is built entirely from chains and a closing stitch, so anyone who can chain can make one.
Difficulty: beginner. If you can chain and slip stitch, you can make a picot.
